rv.q: The fall theater season is still in a fledgling state, but with this marvel of a show it is off to a heartening—make that breathtaking—start.
What it’s missing is its spiritual foil, another note sounding within the din: something to turn the confident period of Stone’s adaptation into an ellipsis.
If a satisfying new “Cherry Orchard” eludes us for now, at least its seedlings are perceptible amid all this poorly pruned old growth.
Unfortunately, the results, while splashily entertaining, feel helium-light instead of morally weighty, with each encounter at once high-stakes and emotionally obvious.
The result is exuberantly theatrical, unexpectedly funny, and alive to the strange comedy that Chekhov always understood could coexist with catastrophe.
If you do know The Cherry Orchard, you’ll be delighted by the way Stone has molded Chekhov’s characters.
The present-day setting is what ultimately makes this Cherry Orchard so tragic.
Newcomers to the play will discover not a bittersweet study in aristocratic stasis so much as a melodrama about the family business.
Yet, there's something fresh here, and vital, an attempt to wrestle in 21st-century terms with Chekhov's themes about an economic system on the brink of collapse.
This Korean Cherry Orchard marks an exceptional new path towards making Chekhov bolder and stronger than ever, even after 125 years.
This adaptation by Simon Stone, which premiered in Seoul, has had subsequent runs in Busan, Hong Kong, Singapore and Australia before arriving here.
Ultimately, the evening thoroughly engages the audience, who are swept up by the emotional and musical language.

cn.t: Stone's Korean-language Cherry Orchard divides critics: some praise its brilliant wit, sumptuous design, and contemporary resonance, while others find it a pretty but overly smooth simplification of Chekhov's tragicomic masterpiece.

vr.q: If you like check off, go check it out for that. If you just like international, seeing things adapted, if you're not afraid of a super title and opening up your perspectives, go go check out the Cherry Orchard
